newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb refugees cram onto train for Bosnia vote.
newsitem.headline: Serb refugees cram onto train for Bosnia vote.

text.p: Hundreds of Serb refugees packed onto an old Yugoslav train in Belgrade on Friday night bound for the Bosnian Serb Republic where they will cast their votes in Bosnia's historic election.
Some were excited at the prospect of the vote, which they hope will finally put the war behind them, but most were confused by the complexity of the poll and unsure who they would vote for.
Around 60,000 refugees living in Serbia are expected to vote in the Bosnian Serb Republic and around 10,000 in the Moslem-Croat Federation.

The first train left Belgrade station at 9.30 p.m., bound for Bijeljina just over the Serbian border from where the refugees will be taken to Brcko by bus. Smoke fogged the windows and the travellers, crammed into carriages, looked blankly out as they pulled away from the platform.
They were preparing for a long, cold night in trains and buses before they could put their cross on a ballot.

Most were elderly, the men dressed in ill-fitting suits and women wrapped up in shawls, thick coats and headscarves. A few young men in black leather jackets and women in high-heeled boots stood out from the crowd.
Tatiana and her husband Predrag, who was holding his three-year-old son Ljubisa, said they were excited about going back to Bosnia to vote.
"We are so happy we're shivering," said Predrag, 31.
They fled from Zivinice, near the northeast Bosnian town of Tuzla, in 1992. "We have no idea what's going to happen. For now we are just taking things one day at a time," he told Reuters.

He said he thought the ultranationalist Serb Democratic Party (SDS) should remain in power in the Serb Republic. "It carried the whole war on its back. The Serb Republic could only survive with the SDS at its head."
He said the refugees in Serbia were doing "the dirtiest kinds of work to survive. But man lives in hope and dies in hope", he added, smiling.
Most refugees seemed less optimistic that Bosnia's first post-war election would lead to the unified country envisaged in the Dayton peace treaty signed last December.

"I have no idea what I will be doing there," said Jovan, 68. A small, grey-haired man with deep wrinkles set into his face, he said nobody had explained to him what the ballot papers would look like and who they would be able to vote for.

"Nobody has explained to us who will be on the list. We have no idea who we will vote for because we have not seen the list (of names on the ballot)," said Mile Kiso, heading for Brcko with his wife Radojka and daughter Sandra, 27.
She studied chemistry in Sarajevo before the war but now has to work like her parents so they can afford their rent and food.
"Frankly, I want her to go and live in Canada, there are no prospects here for her," said her father, a teacher in Bosnia before the war.
A second train pulled into the station shortly after the first one left. Workers from the Red Cross wandered up and down the packed platform as guards directed bewildered refugees.
Around 2,500 people left on the first two trains and more were scheduled to depart throughout the night.
